newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Rebel captors brutalise Ugandan children.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rebel captors brutalise Ugandan children.

text.p: Nearly two years after 12-year-old David O. escaped from his Ugandan captors, he is still traumatised by nightmares.
Images of the scores of children he saw clubbed to death haunt him day and night, along with the painful memory of a young boy he was forced to kill.
"Sometimes, even during the day, I hear him crying for mercy," he told aid workers in Uganda.

David, whose full name was withheld, is one of an estimated 8,000 children abducted by the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) in the last two years, according to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), in what they describe as one of the most serious violations of children's rights in the world.

For while the rest of Uganda moves tentatively towards economic and political stability, UNICEF says the northern districts of Gulu and Kitgum are being torn apart as the Christian fundamentalists loot villages, massacre civilians and kidnap children in a bloody recruitment programme to sustain their army.
Of the 390,000 people in Gulu, 200,000 have been displaced.
"These rebels wander aimlessly throughout Gulu and Kitgum destroying villages, killing countless people and abducting thousands of children," UNICEF's Keith Wright told Reuters.
He said the abducted children are often too scared to try to escape because the rebels are known to follow them home and slaughter their families and friends.
Any children that do escape find it hard to return to normal society, having been forced to kill other children, and sometimes even their sister or brother.
"The psychological trauma is immense," said Wright. "Once you've killed your brother or sister, how can you expect your family to take you back ?"

Many escapees find refuge in a rehabilitation camp at Kiryandongo village run by World Vision, one of UNICEF's partners in the field. Others make their way to one of the Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) detachments which stand guard around villages in Gula and Kitgum from where they will be sent home.
While figures show 4,000 children have escaped from the rebels, Wright said the total abducted was unknown and could be as high as 20,000.
TEENAGE FIGHTING FORCE
The rebels, a mixture of teenage fighting corps and lieutenants in their mid-20's, wander nomadically in groups of around 50. While they do not possess uniforms, most are armed.
They attack anyone riding a bicycle, which is considered to go against the Bible, chopping off limbs or the noses and ears of offenders.

UNICEF says the LRA pull children from their beds, grab them as they dig in fields, and ambush them on their way to collect water. They warn villagers: "Try to find us and we kill them, if they escape we will return to kill you".

The rebels use the children like packhorses to carry loads of up to 30 kg (66 lb), as well as making them do routine chores like cooking. Children who stumble or drop the loads are killed with sticks and stones.
The prettiest girls are selecting to be concubines for the elite officers. The remainder are raped on a daily basis by the fighting corps.
Testimonies obtained by UNICEF from 15 of the escapee children paint a harrowing picture.
"I was forced to be a 'wife' to a big rebel man who I did not like," says a 16-year-old girl known as Janet A. "During the day he would treat me as a prisoner but at night he forced me to love him."

She continues: "I saw a young boy with swollen feet knifed to death because he was so weak and tired he could not walk anymore. He pleaded for mercy as the blood gushed out of his neck but they just laughed."
Other reports tell of children whipped to the bare flesh, stabbed with bayonets and struck with axes. Pregnant girls were beaten if they showed signs of fear when giving birth.
Many died from the meagre and often poisonous diet of leaves, roots, sorghum seeds, grass and even live insects. Others suffered diarrhoea, dysentery and scabies.
BACKGROUND TO THE LORD'S RESISTANCE ARMY
The LRA, which has its roots in the Acholi tribes of Gulu and Kitgum, takes its orders from leader Josef Kony.
Kony took control eight years ago, reshaping what was formerly the Holy Spirit Mobile Force, whose fighters covered themselves with oil in the belief that it would protect them from bullets.
Foremost a religious organisation, the LRA says it wants to rule Uganda in accordance with the Bible's 10 commandments.
The rebels shun the media and negotiations with political leaders.
The only fixed LRA bases are in the south of neighbouring Sudan, which Uganda says supports the rebels.

Sudan not only denies sheltering the rebels, but accuses Uganda of supporting its own rebel movement -- the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) -- whose well-organised troops often clash with the disorderly LRA.
Wright said he believed the LRA was supported in a number of countries.

"There are LRA supporters outside Uganda, not just in Sudan but in London, Toronto, New York and Stockholm," he said. "Inside Uganda, people know it's a big problem, but since it's not considered a major political threat to the rest of the country it gets forgotten about."

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, who says he is committed to resolving the conflict, moved to the north six months ago to direct the war against the rebels but was unable to break their grip on parts of the country. He has since returned to Kampala.
Wright said UNICEF's optimism had increased since Museveni put pressure on Sudan to force the LRA to free 21 schoolgirls kidnapped in October 1996.

Their capture received widespread publicity due to the heroic efforts of teachers who grabbed back 109 of the 139 girls snatched when the LRA stormed into their school. Nine other girls have since broken free.

Earlier this month, UNICEF's Executive Director Carol Bellamy praised the visit to Sudan of a Ugandan delegation to secure the girls' release. The visit resulted in a promise from Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir that the 21 girls would be released imminently.
Further pressure was exerted by Museveni when he boycotted the monthly meeting of the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD) on July 8 and 9.

Officials said Museveni held he would attend only if the girls were returned home. His absence dealt a blow to the five African leaders who had hoped to make progress on ending civil war in Sudan and Somalia in the talks.

"It now looks as if the 21 children will be released unconditionally," said Wright. "We're very optimistic about that, but we want to ensure this is not the closing of the file. We want this to be the start of a continuing flow of children back to their homes."
